#5550. Descope launches Envoy to let consumer apps accept personal AI agents as users

Customer and agentic identity platform company Descope Inc. today launched Envoy, a service that lets consumer websites and apps accept personal artificial intelligence agents acting for their customers without rebuilding how people sign in.

Agents arriving through Envoy get an identity of their own, separate from the customer’s. The launch goes after a choice consumer businesses have been stuck with since agents such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse started shopping and paying for things on people’s behalf.

Amazon.com Inc. blocked Muse from its store in September, saying the agent did not identify itself as one when placing orders, and JPMorgan Chase & Co. moved a month later to keep outside agents away from customer bank accounts. Descope expects blocking will get harder to maintain as more customers do their shopping through an agent.

The alternative, in Descope’s telling, is an agent that signs in as the customer with the person’s own password and one-time code. Nothing in that session shows software was involved, so when a fraud rule fires the logs point at the person. The business ends up absorbing the cost in disputed orders and returns.

Envoy is built around a proposed standard that offers a third option. Meta and Sierra Technologies Inc. published a 0.1 draft of the Personal Agent Protocol in October to set rules for how an agent signs in for someone without posing as them. Under Poppy, as the draft is known, a business publishes the endpoints agents should use and verifies which agent is calling. The business then issues a session bound cryptographically to that agent until the interaction ends.

Developers who adopt Envoy do not have to implement Poppy themselves or keep pace with revisions to it. Descope runs discovery and agent identification, and agents need no advance registration because each one presents a published client metadata document. Session tokens are tied to a key the agent holds through the Demonstrating Proof of Possession standard. Envoy supports all three of the draft’s sign-in types.

Inside Envoy, businesses spell out what an agent is allowed to do on a customer’s account through the Rich Authorization Requests extension to OAuth. In the example Descope gives, a retailer could let a shopping agent place orders for a customer and still keep it away from the payment methods on file. How long any elevated access lasts is left to the retailer as well.

Sensitive actions can go back to the customer for approval on a separate channel, using Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication. Another example from Descope has an agent booking travel hold a fare it found overnight and send the details to the customer’s phone for approval the next morning.

Every token and log entry records the customer and the agent as separate parties, so a company can revoke an agent’s access without signing the customer out. Envoy runs alongside whatever customer identity system a business already has.

Descope co-founder and Chief Executive Slavik Markovich said every login page on the internet was built for a person on the other side, and “that assumption no longer holds true.” In his view, the Personal Agent Protocol is doing for consumer agents what the Model Context Protocol did for enterprise tools.

GoFundMe Inc. and GoodRx Holdings Inc. are among the launch and design partners working with Descope on Envoy over the coming months. Each donation on GoFundMe is “an act of trust,” according to Arnie Katz, the fundraising platform’s chief product and technology officer. He said Envoy will keep the donor and the agent distinct in every session and ask users to approve donations from their phones.

At GoodRx, Chief Technology Officer Nitin Shingate expects people to send agents out to compare pharmacies and find the lowest price on a prescription before they reach the counter. Agents there will get limited permissions covering pricing information.

Agent builders get a tool of their own. A Poppy software development kit, released alongside Envoy, lets any agent work with the protocol, with Descope handling discovery and session management behind it. The kit is written in TypeScript and has no external dependencies.

Envoy sits on top of Descope’s Agentic Identity Hub, which the company updated last month with controls aimed at agents employees build or adopt inside their own organizations. The hub now handles authentication and access control for more than 1,000 MCP servers and millions of agent transactions each month, according to Descope.

Descope is a venture capital-backed startup whose investors include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Notable Capital and Dell Technologies Capital. The company has raised $88 million to date, including a $35 million seed extension in September 2025.

#5549. "Explaining A Decision Is No Longer Enough": Local Governments Face Rising Valuation Appeals, Federal Funding Uncertainty And A Wave Of Retirements In Assessment Offices

The next era of government demands documentation, automation and disciplined execution, the topics of Futureview East

ROCHESTER, N.Y., Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Eagleview, an aerial imagery and geospatial intelligence company, today announced that Futureview East, held in September 2026, at the Louisville Marriott Downtown, brought together 323 local government leaders and partners. As counties and municipalities confront fiscal, legal and workforce pressures and accelerate their use of automation and AI, the conference centered on one priority: to help government officials understand the role of defensible data as they scale automations in both crisis planning and response.

"When a valuation or disaster claim is challenged, an explanation alone does not hold up." - Eagleview CEO

"Local governments are being asked to do more, with less certainty and under closer scrutiny than at any point in recent memory," said Piers Dormeyer, Chief Executive Officer, Eagleview. "When a valuation or disaster claim is challenged, an explanation alone does not hold up. Evidence does. Progress begins with documentation that is accurate, current and defensible."

The conference also marked a milestone for Eagleview: Futureview, first held in Orlando, Florida, in 2006, celebrated its 20th anniversary this year.

Documentation as the first line of defense

In his opening address, Eagleview CEO Piers Dormeyer framed the forces reshaping county and municipal government: uncertainty in federal funding, property tax measures advancing in multiple states, rising valuation appeals, and a retirement wave carrying decades of institutional knowledge out of assessment offices. Valuation appeals are a clear case in point: when a property's assessed value is challenged, the local government must be able to show its work. In this environment, he argued, local governments must do more than explain their decisions. They must be able to prove them.

Automation raises the standard for evidence

Eagleview's product and AI leaders showed how the company is helping customers move from imagery to answers. Its capabilities identify what exists, detect what has changed, explain why it matters and recommend next steps. As more decisions are automated, the integrity of the underlying evidence will determine whether those decisions withstand review.

"Every answer we deliver should be traceable to documentation our customers can stand behind," shared Dylan Kesler, Head of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning at Eagleview.

Bold ambition requires disciplined execution

Keynote speaker Gregory L. Robinson, who led NASA's James Webb Space Telescope program to a successful launch after years of delays, urged attendees to pursue AI, data analytics and other emerging technologies with confidence. Drawing on Webb's turnaround, he emphasized that ambitious programs succeed through culture: transparent communication that rebuilds trust, openness to new ideas, and a disciplined balance between speed and process.

Attendees also reflected on the value of the event:

"I've been to multiple Futureview conferences, and they've always been great. [Eagleview does] a great job, and I'm so glad to be back." â Josh Wadsworth, Washington County, Utah

"This is my first time at this conference, and I can say I'm pleasantly pleased with everything I've seen so far. I was very inspired by Mr. Gregory Robinson's presentation. Not only did it speak to technology, but [it was] also inspirational for those who are in leadership." â Shawnta Privette, Anne Arundel County, Maryland

Continuing the conversation in Fort Worth

To mark Futureview's 20th anniversary and give more customers and partners the opportunity to participate, Eagleview is holding two meetings: Futureview East and Futureview West. The schedule gives organizations flexibility to choose the season that best fits their calendar, recognizing that some government teams have busier fall schedules while others have busier spring schedules.

Futureview West will take place in Fort Worth, Texas, in April 2027. Registration is expected to open in November 2026. Eagleview will share registration details with organizations that have passes.

Eagleview is an industry leader in geospatial intelligence (GeoAI) delivering AI-powered property intelligence solutions that enable customers across a broad range of industries to accurately explore properties and structures, identify and implement solutions today, and find tomorrow's opportunities. For more than 25 years, Eagleview has built proprietary property imaging technology earning more than 300+ patents and generating over 3.5 billion high-resolution images resulting in a library that encompasses 96% of the U.S. population. With Eagleview's trusted insights, customers can make business decisions that matter.

#5548. The deal closed. When do the savings start?

For homebuilders, the timing of acquisition savings often comes down to the systems and Supplier connections already in place

Purchasing synergies can materially improve homebuilder acquisition savings and strengthen the economics of the deal. They can also be overstated when the deal model doesn’t fully reflect the cost and time required to achieve them.

Combining the purchasing volume of two builders should create leverage for better pricing and stronger margins. But before that leverage is real, someone has to determine what each company is buying, how their supplier agreements differ and what it will take to operate under a common set of processes.

That’s where the financial projections meet the realities of running the business.

I’ve worked on acquisition diligence and integration across different industries, and the question I believe deserves more attention isn’t how much a deal can save. It’s when those savings actually show up in the P&L. For homebuilders, technology has a significant role in the solution. Buying power only matters if you can use it Consider a builder acquiring a regional operation with established supplier relationships and a healthy pipeline of homes under construction. The opportunity is clear. The combined company is buying more materials across more communities, which should create leverage to negotiate better terms. Now look at what has to happen to capture those savings. The acquired company may use a different ERP, organize its purchasing data differently or have supplier agreements that don’t align with the parent company’s contracts. Before purchasing leadership can negotiate from a position of combined volume, they need an accurate, combined view of what that volume actually is. Meanwhile, both businesses still have homes to build. Construction schedules can’t be put on hold while systems are reconciled. It’s entirely possible to have a sound purchasing strategy and spend the first several months after closing working through the operational issues that prevent successful execution. As builders know better than anyone, these delays carry real cost. If the acquisition model assumes purchasing savings will start contributing to margin within two quarters and integration takes a year, you won’t get the return you underwrote. The savings may still arrive, but every quarter of delay is value that doesn’t come back. This matters even more when interest rates are high. There’s usually a second cost hiding in the same delay: running two sets of systems, two sets of processes and often two teams doing the same work until integration is complete. Those dual running costs rarely get the same scrutiny as the synergy number. Homebuilder M&A integration is a financial decision Technology deserves a more prominent place in acquisition diligence and homebuilder M&A integration, particularly when operating efficiencies account for a meaningful share of the expected return. Knowing which applications a company runs is a starting point. The more important question is how those systems will work inside the larger organization, and what it will cost to get them there. Can the acquiring builder get reliable purchasing data across both businesses on day one? Can existing systems exchange the information needed to keep construction moving? What will it cost to maintain separate environments while integration is underway, and for how long? These sound like operating questions. They’re also valuation questions. The same applies to proprietary technology. Many builders have invested heavily in systems developed specifically for their businesses, and there can be good reasons for doing so. The challenge arises when those systems must accommodate an organization they weren’t originally designed to support. Custom integrations require people and capital to build. They also require ongoing security and maintenance as the business changes, and that cost doesn’t end when the integration goes live. I want to understand those costs before committing to an acquisition, not discover them in the first integration budget review. The advantage of an established network One factor that is often overlooked in technology discussions is the value of connectivity that already exists. A homebuilding operation depends on relationships with suppliers, manufacturers and trades that extend well beyond its internal systems. Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we’ve spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn’t starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder’s suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that’s the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren’t onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. Supplier contracts have to be evaluated, processes aligned and technology decisions made. No platform eliminates those responsibilities. But when connections and integrations are already in place, there’s less to build, and the combined company gets to consolidated purchasing sooner. From a financial standpoint, that shows up in two places: lower cost to achieve, and a shorter path to realized savings. Put a timeline behind the savings Acquisition models typically do a good job of identifying where value can be created. I would encourage builders to apply the same discipline to understanding what it will take to capture the expected value, and how much time and risk stand between the deal and the savings. If the investment thesis depends on consolidated purchasing, define what has to happen before the company can actually operate that way. Put a cost on the technology requirements. Build a realistic integration timeline into the model and align the timing of purchasing synergies with it. And ask these questions before an acquisition is on the table. The same infrastructure that supports integration also determines how efficiently a builder expands into new markets or adds divisions organically. For a CFO, the synergy number is only part of the picture. The timing and the cost to achieve it matter just as much to the investment decision. Before signing off on an expected savings number, I want to understand what has to change in the business for that number to become real. If technology integration is part of the answer, it needs to be part of the financial plan. Learn more about Hyphen Solutions and its connected residential construction network Click Here Related

If the acquisition model assumes purchasing savings will start contributing to margin within two quarters and integration takes a year, you won’t get the return you underwrote. The savings may still arrive, but every quarter of delay is value that doesn’t come back. This matters even more when interest rates are high. There’s usually a second cost hiding in the same delay: running two sets of systems, two sets of processes and often two teams doing the same work until integration is complete. Those dual running costs rarely get the same scrutiny as the synergy number. Homebuilder M&A integration is a financial decision Technology deserves a more prominent place in acquisition diligence and homebuilder M&A integration, particularly when operating efficiencies account for a meaningful share of the expected return. Knowing which applications a company runs is a starting point. The more important question is how those systems will work inside the larger organization, and what it will cost to get them there. Can the acquiring builder get reliable purchasing data across both businesses on day one? Can existing systems exchange the information needed to keep construction moving? What will it cost to maintain separate environments while integration is underway, and for how long? These sound like operating questions. They’re also valuation questions. The same applies to proprietary technology. Many builders have invested heavily in systems developed specifically for their businesses, and there can be good reasons for doing so. The challenge arises when those systems must accommodate an organization they weren’t originally designed to support. Custom integrations require people and capital to build. They also require ongoing security and maintenance as the business changes, and that cost doesn’t end when the integration goes live. I want to understand those costs before committing to an acquisition, not discover them in the first integration budget review. The advantage of an established network One factor that is often overlooked in technology discussions is the value of connectivity that already exists. A homebuilding operation depends on relationships with suppliers, manufacturers and trades that extend well beyond its internal systems. Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we’ve spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn’t starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder’s suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that’s the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren’t onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. Supplier contracts have to be evaluated, processes aligned and technology decisions made. No platform eliminates those responsibilities. But when connections and integrations are already in place, there’s less to build, and the combined company gets to consolidated purchasing sooner. From a financial standpoint, that shows up in two places: lower cost to achieve, and a shorter path to realized savings. Put a timeline behind the savings Acquisition models typically do a good job of identifying where value can be created. I would encourage builders to apply the same discipline to understanding what it will take to capture the expected value, and how much time and risk stand between the deal and the savings. If the investment thesis depends on consolidated purchasing, define what has to happen before the company can actually operate that way. Put a cost on the technology requirements. Build a realistic integration timeline into the model and align the timing of purchasing synergies with it. And ask these questions before an acquisition is on the table. The same infrastructure that supports integration also determines how efficiently a builder expands into new markets or adds divisions organically. For a CFO, the synergy number is only part of the picture. The timing and the cost to achieve it matter just as much to the investment decision. Before signing off on an expected savings number, I want to understand what has to change in the business for that number to become real. If technology integration is part of the answer, it needs to be part of the financial plan. Learn more about Hyphen Solutions and its connected residential construction network Click Here Related

Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we’ve spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn’t starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder’s suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that’s the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren’t onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. Supplier contracts have to be evaluated, processes aligned and technology decisions made. No platform eliminates those responsibilities. But when connections and integrations are already in place, there’s less to build, and the combined company gets to consolidated purchasing sooner. From a financial standpoint, that shows up in two places: lower cost to achieve, and a shorter path to realized savings. Put a timeline behind the savings Acquisition models typically do a good job of identifying where value can be created. I would encourage builders to apply the same discipline to understanding what it will take to capture the expected value, and how much time and risk stand between the deal and the savings. If the investment thesis depends on consolidated purchasing, define what has to happen before the company can actually operate that way. Put a cost on the technology requirements. Build a realistic integration timeline into the model and align the timing of purchasing synergies with it. And ask these questions before an acquisition is on the table. The same infrastructure that supports integration also determines how efficiently a builder expands into new markets or adds divisions organically. For a CFO, the synergy number is only part of the picture. The timing and the cost to achieve it matter just as much to the investment decision. Before signing off on an expected savings number, I want to understand what has to change in the business for that number to become real. If technology integration is part of the answer, it needs to be part of the financial plan. Learn more about Hyphen Solutions and its connected residential construction network Click Here Related

#5547. Anthropic’s Claude AI Predicts a Massive BTC USD Move

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin (BTC) might not need another halving, another wave of institutional adoption, or even another round of monetary easing to deliver one of its most explosive rallies yet. Anthropic’s Claude AI predicts that it might need something considerably bigger: a fundamental shift in how the world’s largest economies treat Bitcoin.

Imagine the United States announcing a landmark expansion of its strategic Bitcoin reserve, followed by several major sovereign wealth funds committing billions of dollars to BTC.

Add a deterioration in confidence in traditional government debt and a sudden rush towards alternative stores of value, and Bitcoin could find itself at the center of an extraordinary financial realignment.

The most explosive scenario would begin with Washington committing to actively accumulate Bitcoin rather than simply retaining its existing seized holdings. An official purchasing program, potentially paired with incentives for allied nations to build their own reserves, could fundamentally change Bitcoin’s investment narrative.

The potential domino effect would be enormous:

Government adoption: The US establishes a long-term Bitcoin accumulation strategy, encouraging other nations to follow.

Sovereign wealth funds: Major investment funds in the Middle East and Asia begin allocating even small percentages of their portfolios to BTC.

Institutional FOMO: Pension funds, insurance companies, and asset managers accelerate allocations to avoid being left behind.

Monetary easing: Deteriorating government debt markets force central banks towards looser monetary policy, potentially increasing demand for scarce assets.

Bitcoin’s fixed supply of 21 million coins makes this particularly interesting. With approximately 450 new BTC entering circulation daily, a sudden acceleration in institutional and sovereign demand could create a substantial supply-demand imbalance.

From a technical perspective, Bitcoin would first need to reclaim the $80,000-$85,000 region and establish it as support. A sustained breakout above $90,000 would provide a much stronger bullish signal, potentially attracting momentum traders and sidelined institutional capital.

Beyond that, the $100,000 psychological milestone would become the next major battleground. A convincing weekly breakout, accompanied by expanding trading volume, a bullish MACD crossover, and RSI momentum returning to stronger territory, could provide the foundations for another major price discovery phase.

If institutional inflows accelerated alongside these developments, Bitcoin could potentially target $150,000 before entering an even more aggressive speculative rally.

The final leg towards $250,000 would require an extraordinary combination of sovereign adoption, institutional FOMO, and favorable macroeconomic conditions. This is not a technical outcome we can currently assume; it would depend heavily on the hypothetical catalyst materializing.

#5546. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5545. Precision 360 Degree Approach to GLP-1 Management Helps Reduce Costs for Employers, Improves Results for Employees

Payer Matrix, Cecelia Health and Blue Genes Lab partner to combine genetic screening, clinical support and approval oversight with brand-name GLP-1s at half the price of standard coverage

PHOENIX, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Payer Matrix, Cecelia Health and Blue Genes Lab today announced a new integrated medication management program, PreciselyRx, to help self-funded employers manage GLP-1 coverage from the first prescription through the first year of therapy.

Obesity is a leading driver of chronic conditions, such as diabetes and heart disease. GLP-1 medications can help many people achieve meaningful weight loss, but their costâup to a third of an employer's annual prescription drug spendâcreates difficult coverage decisions for employers. Managing that investment requires more than controlling the price of each prescription; it also requires informed treatment decisions and support throughout therapy. PreciselyRx enables employers to capture the health benefits and medical cost savings associated with brand name GLP-1s at approximately half the cost of standard GLP-1 coverage.

PreciselyRx addresses four major sources of medication-related waste by combining rigorous approval controls, pre-treatment genetic screening, sourcing at the lowest available net cost, and 12 months of clinical support. #5544. Beyond the credit report: How lenders can navigate the next era of mortgage credit

Advantage Partners Solutions’ Patrick Tynan explains why new scoring options, rising costs and evolving credit requirements are changing how lenders approach mortgage credit strategy.

New scoring models, evolving credit requirements and persistent cost pressures are forcing mortgage lenders to rethink their mortgage credit strategy. As the industry moves toward more flexible credit scoring, lenders must balance potential savings with risk, operational efficiency and borrower access.

In this conversation, Patrick Tynan, Chief Sales Officer at Advantage Partners Solutions (APS), discusses the impact of VantageScore 4.0, why cost per funded loan matters more than individual credit report pricing and how strategic CRA partnerships can help lenders prepare for what comes next.

HousingWire: Mortgage credit is entering a period of significant change, with new scoring models and continued cost pressure. Which shifts do you believe will have the greatest impact on lenders, and where should they be paying closer attention?

Patrick Tynan: One of the biggest changes I have seen in my career is happening right now, and it is VantageScore 4.0. For decades, lenders had one option. Now they have a real choice. Lenders can use VantageScore 4.0 today on most loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and FHA begins accepting it on January 1.

I am a big believer in it. VantageScore 4.0 builds trended data into its scoring algorithm, so it can score borrowers who have thin files or who have worked hard to improve their credit. That means more people getting into homes without anyone lowering the bar, and it delivers significant savings compared with what lenders pay today.

Where I would tell lenders to slow down is the push to collect less information on the borrower. There is a lot of talk about pulling fewer bureaus, and I understand the appeal. But saving a few dollars by seeing less of the borrower is not a good trade. My advice is to take advantage of the new score option and keep the tri-merge credit report.

HW: As lenders evaluate adopting VantageScore 4.0 and other changes to the credit landscape, how should they balance potential cost savings with adapting workflows, implementation and borrower experience?

PT: Here is what I tell every lender I sit down with: When it comes to credit, there is no one-size-fits-all. A shop doing heavy purchase business with a lot of preapprovals runs completely differently than one with strong pull-through. Some lenders come out ahead paying per report. Others save a lot more with a bundled approach.

That is why we do not just hand someone a price sheet. We are a partner, not just a company that sells credit reports. We learn how a lender does business and build the pricing structure that saves them the most money and runs the most efficiently. The number I care about is cost per funded loan, not cost per pull, because only about one in five pulls ever closes. From there, make sure your systems, investors and MI partners are ready for VantageScore 4.0 and for FICO 10T down the road.

HW: As credit becomes more complex, how is the relationship between lenders and their credit providers evolving beyond a transactional service? What should lenders expect from a strategic CRA partner today?

PT: I came up on the lending side, managing teams at Wells Fargo and Countrywide, before I ever worked for a vendor. So, I know what it feels like to be the lender waiting on a report with a closing on the line. What has changed is that lenders need a lot more than a fast, accurate report now. They are deciding which score to use, how many bureaus to pull and when to pull them, and the rules keep moving under their feet. That is where a real partner earns their keep.

Tell them what a new rule means for their shop. Deliver the scores they need from all three bureaus without making them rip out their technology. Show them where every credit dollar is going. And answer the phone when a rescore is holding up a closing. If your credit provider only shows up when the invoice does, you do not have a partner. You have a vendor.

HW: Advantage Partners Solutions combines scale with a privately held structure and capabilities beyond credit reporting. How does that position APS to support lenders differently as market and vendor dynamics continue to shift?

PT: Advantage Partners Solutions is one of the top five credit resellers in the country by revenue, but we are one of the rare companies at that level that is privately held rather than owned by private equity or publicly traded. Our job is to bring the three bureaus together for our clients. Because we are not a bureau ourselves, we are not tied to any one source of data, so we can give lenders the complete tri-merge picture with whatever scoring model fits their business best – that independence matters to us. We make decisions based on what our clients need, not on an investor’s timeline or a quarterly earnings call, and that lets us move early.

VantageScore 4.0 is a good example of how we move early and in the best interests of our clients. We believed lenders and borrowers should have options, so we moved quickly to offer it.

Also, bringing Advantage Credit and Partners Credit & Verifications together gave us the scale to keep investing in technology and people, so our clients are not rebuilding workflows every time the rules shift. It also means we are a fully stocked provider of credit, verification services, flood certifications, and a full suite of QC products with the same breadth lenders expect from the largest companies in our industry. Lenders can rely on one partner across more of the loan file instead of managing a long list of vendors.

HW: Looking ahead, what changes do you expect to reshape mortgage credit over the next several years, and what should lenders be doing now to make sure their credit strategy can adapt?

PT: A few years from now, I think having multiple score options will simply be how business gets done. More data, such as rent payments and other nontraditional tradelines, will feed into scoring, but the cost pressure is not going away. The rules are still moving, too.

FHFA has said it is reviewing both the credit report requirement and loan-level pricing, so lenders should expect more change, and likely soon. With that said, our positions is simple: keep the tri-merge. It is the safest and fairest way to evaluate a borrower, and there are smarter ways to save money than pulling less data.

My advice is not to wait for a final rule. We are actively working with our lenders to create a mortgage credit strategy. We are making sure our technology is ready for VantageScore 4.0. The lenders who do that work now will be the ones ahead when the next announcement comes.

#5543. Rogervoice Brings Free, Real-Time Captioning to In-Person Conversations

The captioning app for calls and in-person conversations now helps users follow everyday conversations in real time, with saved transcripts and on-device captioning that works offline.

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rogervoice, the AI-powered captioning app, today announced the launch of free in-person captioning. The new feature brings real-time captions and saved transcripts to face-to-face conversations, helping users keep up with the moments that matter, from work meetings and doctor's appointments to dinners with friends and family.

Not every conversation happens on the phone. There's the client lunch where someone rattles off a deadline, the pharmacy counter where you need to catch every detail, or catching up with a friend or family member. Rogervoice's new in-person captioning feature lets users read along as conversations happen, so they can stay in the moment and revisit the details afterward.

"I used to rely on two separate apps for phone calls and for meetings or in-person events. Now Rogervoice has everything in one place, which makes it so much simpler. I love that the captions are real-time, just like on my calls, and that they're saved so I can go back to them whenever I need. As someone who is hard of hearing, having real-time captions makes everything easier," said Brittany M., a Rogervoice user.

Available through the new Live tab in the Rogervoice app, in-person captioning is simple to use: open the app, start a session, and let the conversation unfold. Speech appears in real time in an adjustable, full-width caption area designed for readability. Captioning runs directly on the user's phone, works offline and is available in 45 languages on iPhone and 15 on Android. Afterward, users can revisit and export their saved transcripts.

"Earlier this year in our State of the Phone Call Survey, we found that 60% of Americans believe phone calls are not fully accessible to people who are deaf or hard of hearing. But conversations don't stop at the end of a call. People need to keep up at work, at the doctor's office and with the people they love. We built Rogervoice around that reality, and in-person captioning is another way to help people stay connected and keep moving on their own terms," said Olivier Jeannel, founder of Rogervoice, who has been deaf since age two.

The launch builds on Rogervoice's continued growth and recognition in 2026. Founded in 2014, the company has captioned more than 12 million calls in over 100 languages. Over the past few months, Rogervoice won The A.I. Awards (AI for Good) and the Hearing Technology Innovator Award (Captioning Technologies: Mobile Apps), was named as a finalist in The Anthem Awards and ranked No. 3 on TechRound's US50 list of American startups to watch.

Rogervoice brings phone-call and in-person captioning together in one app. Captioned calls are FCC-certified and free for eligible users, while in-person captioning is free. Captioning is AI-only, with no human listener on calls, no ads and no data sold. In-person captioning works offline and on-device, so conversation data never leaves the user's phone.

To download the free app, visit the App Store and Google Play, or go to rogervoice.com/app.

TAICHUNG, Taiwan, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Winbond Electronics Corporation, a leading global supplier of semiconductor memory solutions, today announced the CRA Conformance and Integration Kit for its TrustMEÂ® W77Q Secure Flash family. The package is designed to help manufacturers accelerate readiness for the European Union's Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) by providing hardware security, software, integration guidance, testing resources, reference designs, and security evidence in a unified package.

The CRA introduces cybersecurity requirements across the lifecycle of products with digital elements, covering areas including secure design and development, production, vulnerability handling, software maintenance, and technical documentation. Winbond's CRA Conformance and Integration Kit helps customers translate these requirements into implementation and system-level verification activities.

TrustMEÂ® W77Q Secure Flash has achieved SESIP Level 2 certification, providing independently assessed security evidence to support customers in evaluating the component's security and their own product-level compliance activities. Component-level certification does not by itself establish CRA conformity of the finished product.

For platforms already using external NOR Flash, W77Q can provide a practical migration path where package, voltage, interface, and system requirements align. While integration may require hardware and software changes, W77Q can strengthen external memory security without adding a separate security component or requiring a complete platform redesign.

The W77Q CRA Conformance and Integration Kit brings together key resources to support implementation, testing, and documentation, including:

Supporting Long-Lifecycle and Post-Quantum Security

The CRA Integration Kit also builds on Winbond's post-quantum cryptography (PQC) work for Secure Flash. Supported W77Q devices use the Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) scheme specified in NIST SP 800-208 to authenticate firmware and software updates.

W77Q security capabilitiesâincluding protected storage, authenticated software updates, version enforcement, rollback protection, and recoveryâsupport security throughout the product lifecycle. These capabilities can help OEMs address security requirements for long-life connected products while providing a path to PQC-protected update authentication where supported by the selected device and system architecture.

"The Cyber Resilience Act makes cybersecurity a lifecycle responsibility. Our CRA Conformance and Integration Kit brings together Secure Flash, software, validation assets, and reusable security evidence to help customers integrate security functions and document their designs. W77Q's SESIP certification provides independent assessment of the component, helping customers establish a stronger foundation for their own product-level compliance activities," said Winbond.

"Complying with the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is challenging because manufacturers must verify how third-party components meet system-level security requirements. Winbond's W77Q Secure Flash and CRA Integration Kit solve this challenge by providing hardware-enforced security capabilities alongside comprehensive integration guidance, testing tools, and structured documentation. This ready-to-use compliance evidence streamlines the due diligence process and significantly reduces the engineering effort required for both internal self-assessments and third-party conformity audits," said JosÃ© Pulido, Director at jtsec Beyond IT Security.

The Winbond CRA Conformance and Integration Kit is designed for connected products across industrial automation, Industrial IoT, networking, smart building and access control, HVAC, energy, EV charging, smart appliances, and other applications requiring secure lifecycle management and CRA readiness.

For more information about Winbond Secure Flash products and solutions, please visit the Winbond website.

Winbond was established in September 1987 and listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in 1995. The company is headquartered at the Central Taiwan Science Park (CTSP) in Taichung, Taiwan, and operates two highly automated and intelligent 12-inch wafer fabs in Taichung and Kaohsiung. Winbond is committed to providing comprehensive integrated circuit solutions to customers worldwide, with major product lines including Code Storage Flash, Customized Memory Solution (CMS), and various logic IC solutions.

#5540. New Research: 92% of HR Professionals Believe Employees Can Be Reskilled for AI Jobs, Yet External Hiring Outpaces Redeployment

â Survey of more than 1,100 U.S. HR professionals and people managers reveals a disconnect between confidence in existing talent and AI workforce hiring practices â

WILMINGTON, Del., Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Despite widespread confidence that existing employees can be trained for jobs created by artificial intelligence, organizations are more likely to hire externally than redeploy workers already on their payroll, according to new research from Careerminds, a leading global provider of workforce solutions.

The findings, published in Careerminds' new white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, reveal that 92% of HR professionals and 88% of people managers believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles. Yet 51% of HR professionals and 47% of people managers report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions, compared with just 42% in each group who report redeploying existing employees.

Careerminds' new research: 92% of HR pros say staff can be reskilled for AI, yet external hiring outpaces redeployment.

The research, conducted in partnership with Censuswide, surveyed 1,142 U.S. HR professionals and people managers at organizations with 500 or more employees.

"Companies are investing in AI while potentially overlooking one of their most valuable resources: the people they already employ," said Mark Saddic, Senior Partner at Careerminds. "Our research shows that organizations largely believe their employees can adapt to AI-driven change, but that confidence isn't consistently translating into opportunities. Before looking outside the organization, leaders need to understand the skills they already have, identify where employees can grow, and establish a clear process for making those transitions possible."

Confidence in Reskilling Isn't Translating Into Action

One potential barrier is a lack of visibility into employees' existing skills and potential. According to the research, approximately 43% of HR professionals and 34% of people managers report limited visibility or uncertainty about which employees should be reskilled.

At the same time, 87% of HR professionals and 84% of people managers believe their organizations adequately consider reskilling employees for future roles. The findings suggest that organizations may believe they are prioritizing internal talent development even when their hiring practices tell a different story.

HR and Managers Disagree About Who Owns AI Workforce Planning

The study also reveals significant disagreement over who is responsible for managing AI's impact on the workforce.

Nearly two-thirds (63%) of HR professionals believe HR has primary responsibility for planning and managing AI-driven workforce changes. However, only 24% of people managers agree. Instead, 35% of managers point to senior leadership outside HR.

This disconnect could complicate efforts to identify internal talent, coordinate reskilling programs, and transition employees into emerging roles.

The findings also reveal significant differences in how industries are responding to AI-related workforce needs.

In Technology and Telecom, external hiring outpaces redeployment by 15 percentage points among both HR professionals and people managers.

By contrast, Media and Entertainment is the only sector surveyed where both groups report redeployment at least as frequently as external hiring. Among HR professionals in that industry, 56% report redeploying employees compared with just 25% hiring externally.

The implications extend beyond workforce planning. Separate research from The Josh Bersin Company, cited in the Careerminds white paper, indicates that external hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally and take up to 20 days longer.

Careerminds recommends that organizations establish clear accountability for AI workforce planning, improve visibility into existing employee skills, and evaluate opportunities for internal development before defaulting to external recruitment.

The full white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, is available at https://careerminds.com/redeployment-gap.

Methodology: Careerminds partnered with Censuswide to survey 595 U.S. HR professionals and 547 U.S. people managers, ages 25â65, working at organizations with 500 to 10,000 or more employees. The research was conducted May 15â26, 2026.

#5539. Qloo's Global Agentic Hackathon Draws Nearly 3,000 Developers, as Jason Calacanis pledges to invest in winner

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Qloo, a leading artificial intelligence company providing taste intelligence for AI agents and consumer experiences , today announced that nearly 3,000 developers worldwide participated in its Global Agentic Hackathon, building functional AI applications powered by Qloo's technology. The competition will culminate November 5, when the finalists present their applications live on entrepreneur and investor Jason Calacanis's This Week in Startups podcast, where judges will select a winner.

The competition's judging panel brings together prominent leaders across technology, investment, entertainment, and business, including Calacanis, entrepreneur and angel investor; Cedric the Entertainer, actor and comedian; Nicole Seligman, member of the OpenAI Board of Directors; Todd Boehly, co-founder and CEO of Eldridge Industries; Michael Abrams, EVP of Strategic Initiatives at Live Nation Entertainment; and Mike Diolosa, CTO of Qloo.

Hosted on Devpost, the Qloo Agentic Hackathon challenged developers to build functional AI agents and applications using Qloo's Taste AI infrastructure to understand consumer preferences and deliver more personalized recommendations. The competition awarded $25,000 in prizes across the top three submissions: $15,000 for first place, $6,000 for second place, and $4,000 for third place. Separately, Calacanis has pledged a personal investment of $25,000 in his favorite project, creating an opportunity for a participating team to secure early-stage backing and take its application beyond the competition.

Unlike traditional hackathons that may focus on concepts or prototypes, the competition required participants to submit functional, externally hosted applications integrating Qloo's API, along with public code repositories and documentation. The goal was to identify practical applications demonstrating how cultural intelligence can make AI agents more useful in real-world consumer experiences.

The hackathon comes as technology companies explore how AI agents can move beyond answering questions to making decisions and completing purchases on behalf of consumers. While agents can increasingly search for products, compare options, and carry out transactions, understanding individual preferences remains a significant challenge, particularly when limited information is available.

For example, an AI travel agent may be able to find flights, compare hotels, and book restaurant reservations. But determining which hotel, restaurant, or experience best matches an individual's tastes requires a different kind of intelligence. Preferences are shaped by everything from entertainment and dining habits to cultural interests and lifestyle choices, and those connections are not always apparent from a single request.

Qloo's Taste AI technology is designed to address this challenge. Its proprietary data and AI models identify relationships across consumer interests, drawing on a cultural knowledge graph spanning more than 600 million entities across music, film, dining, fashion, travel, and other categories. This infrastructure enables developers and large enterprises to incorporate taste-based intelligence into applications at scale without relying on personally identifiable information, giving AI agents additional context to inform recommendations and decisions based on what consumers are likely to enjoy.

As AI agents increasingly become intermediaries between consumers and businesses, understanding individual preferences could become a critical component of agentic commerce. An agent may be able to execute a transaction, but its ability to understand a consumer's cultural preferences can determine whether its recommendations are relevant in the first place. Qloo's technology provides the taste intelligence layer for those decisions , helping developers build agents that understand not just what consumers ask for, but what they are likely to value.

"AI agents are getting better at completing tasks, but there's still a big difference between knowing how to book a trip and knowing what kind of trip someone would actually enjoy," said Michael Diolosa, CTO of Qloo. "That's where taste intelligence becomes essential infrastructure. We're seeing developers use Qloo to build agents that can make decisions based on individual preferences, even when they have very little information to start with. The response to this hackathon shows the appetite for that intelligence and the opportunity to build new businesses around it."

#5537. Assail Introduces Cassandra, a Proactive AI Agent Connecting Threat Modeling with Autonomous Security Testing

New capabilities in Ares identify emerging exposures, prioritize security assessments, and connect attack scenarios to validated findings and remediation verification.

BOSTON, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Assail, Inc., a developer of sovereign AI-powered offensive security platforms, today announced Cassandraâ¢, a proactive AI agent integrated into its Aresâ¢ platform, alongside expanded threat modeling capabilities that connect attack scenarios directly to autonomous security testing and remediation verification.

Cassandra continuously monitors changes across an organization's attack surface, identifies emerging exposures, prioritizes security activities, and prepares assessment and retest plans. Combined with Ares Threat Models, these capabilities help security teams move beyond identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding which attack paths can be exploited, what requires attention, and whether remediation efforts have been successful.

Unlike traditional security tools that rely on periodic assessments and disconnected reporting, Ares connects threat modeling, autonomous testing, and verification in a coordinated workflow. Cassandra serves as the proactive intelligence layer, identifying changes and recommending next steps while keeping operators in control of testing decisions.

"Security teams need to know what attackers can exploit and whether their fixes work. We built Cassandra and threat modeling into Ares to help them answer those questions and act on the results," said Alissa Knight, CEO of Assail. "We're connecting those two disciplines inside Ares. Cassandra helps teams decide what to test next. Ares tests it, shows what attackers can exploit, and checks whether the fixes work."

Cassandra: Turning Security Intelligence into Action

Cassandra introduces a proactive approach to security operations by bringing critical exposures, attack surface changes, and recommended actions directly into the Ares operator experience.

Using existing assessment findings, asset information, and discovery results, Cassandra identifies newly exposed APIs, critical vulnerabilities, previously remediated issues that have resurfaced, and newly discovered assets. She explains why changes matter, connects findings to supporting evidence, and recommends appropriate next steps.

Security teams can use Cassandra to summarize recent activity, identify outstanding risks, prepare assessment and retest plans, and coordinate follow-up through Ares, email, or Slack. Cassandra also maintains operator-defined restrictions, including excluded targets and deferred testing activities.

Organizations retain operational control through configurable modes: Brief Only, Draft for Me, and Act on Approval. Every assessment initiated through Cassandra requires human approval and remains subject to authorization, permissions, and established scope controls.

Importantly, Cassandra distinguishes completed assessments from interrupted or failed testing, ensuring incomplete results are not mistaken for evidence that a system is secure.

Threat Models: Connecting Attack Scenarios to Evidence

Ares Threat Models extends traditional threat modeling by connecting potential attack scenarios to the results of authorized autonomous security assessments.

Security teams can map application components, system relationships, sensitive data, and potential attack paths, whether evaluating an existing application or a system still in development. Ares then translates relevant scenarios into testing objectives, helping teams determine which threats are exploitable and which remain unverified.

Assessment results feed directly into the threat model, distinguishing successful attacks, unsuccessful attempts, and scenarios requiring additional testing. Findings remain connected to supporting evidence, corrective actions, and subsequent verification.

As environments change, Ares incorporates new assessment evidence while preserving customer-authored scenarios and decisions. Proposed AI-generated changes to system diagrams remain subject to operator review, ensuring teams maintain control over their security models and risk decisions.

A Continuous Cycle of Discovery, Testing, and Verification

Together, Cassandra and Threat Models establish a connected process for identifying exposures, validating attack scenarios, and verifying remediation.

For example, when Ares discovers an undocumented API endpoint, Cassandra can flag the exposure and associate it with an existing authorization threat. Ares can then execute an approved assessment, attach the findings to the relevant threat scenario, and update the model. Following remediation, Cassandra can prepare a retest plan for operator approval.

This integrated approach reduces the disconnect between what security teams believe could happen, what autonomous testing demonstrates, and what remains unresolved.

Cassandra and Threat Models operate within Ares, Assail's expeditionary offensive security platform designed for enterprise and mission-critical environments.

Through Assail Anywhereâ¢, organizations can deploy the platform and its AI model through SaaS, within their own cloud infrastructure, on-premises, or in disconnected and air-gapped environments. This deployment flexibility enables organizations to maintain control over sensitive data, testing operations, and AI infrastructure without sacrificing autonomous security capabilities.

#5536. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

Event explores the priorities shaping financial services as institutions balance innovation, resilience, and growth

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Finastra's third Innovating Finance Together Summit, held in New York, brought together financial industry leaders and innovators from across North America to explore the trends shaping lending, trade, and payments.

A central theme was that financial institutions are entering a new phase of modernization, where success is defined not by deploying new technology, but by extracting greater value from existing investments. Throughout the event, speakers highlighted that adoption has not necessarily kept pace with innovation, particularly as institutions navigate the convergence of AI, security, geopolitical volatility and evolving payments infrastructure.

Institutions should focus investment on a smaller, core portfolio, modernize existing platforms to improve interoperability, and use AI to deliver operational efficiencies while maintaining security, resilience and reliable money movement. Existing instant payments infrastructure remains underutilized, highlighting the need for modern API-based architecture and accessible data to support sustainable growth.

"What struck me most was how much common ground there is across the industry.  Banks want to innovate, but they also need to get more from the technology they already have while ensuring that their systems remain secure, reliable, and resilient. The conversation is shifting from what's possible to what actually delivers value for customers.  And that's exactly where it should be," said Chris Walters, CEO, Finastra."

Security and resilience emerged as critical priorities as financial institutions continue to modernize. As cyber threats become more sophisticated, financial institutions need technology environments that can adapt quickly, address vulnerabilities, and maintain resilience. Modern architecture can make it easier to deliver updates, strengthen security, and respond to emerging risks.

AI presents significant opportunities across lending, payments, and other banking operations, particularly where document handling, verification, and decision-making create bottlenecks across the workflow. Speakers emphasized the importance of starting with a clear business problem, rather than deploying AI for its own sake.  Success depends on understanding existing workflows, identifying where AI can make a difference, and keeping people involved in critical decisions, with security governance and accountability built in.

The underlying message was clear: extract value from the technology you have now. Competitive advantages will come from making smarter technology investments and getting more from existing systems while modernizing infrastructure, improving interoperability and adopting new capabilities that deliver measurable value.

#5534. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.
