#5493. The best travel gear of 2026, according to Shop TODAY

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A selection of 15 winners from Shop TODAY's 2026 Travel Awards, from a $39.90 Uniqlo dress to a Quince carry-on and a Qi2 charger.

Every trip starts with a zipper and a hope. A traveler closes the bag, heads for the door, and trusts that nothing inside will give out between the curb and the destination. Gear draws little attention until it breaks. A strap snaps in a terminal, a phone dies before the boarding call, or an outfit that looked fine at home turns sticky and heavy in the afternoon heat. Small objects carry outsized consequences once a traveler leaves home behind. The right pieces fade into the background and let the trip unfold. The wrong ones become the story people tell after they unpack.

The friction piles up in ways no packing list captures. Airlines tack fees onto bags, and each additional one adds to the bill. Outlets abroad come in unfamiliar setups that an everyday charger may not fit. Necklaces and earrings knot themselves into clumps inside a pouch. A delayed layover can stretch into an unplanned overnight stay that leaves a passenger too anxious to sleep. Stacked over a week, these snags drain the energy, money, and patience a person on the road would prefer to spend on the place itself. Many of them yield to better equipment, provided someone has put it through real use before departure.

Shop TODAY editors spent months putting clothing, tech, luggage, and accessories through trials for the outlet's fourth annual Travel Awards. Candidates came from new launches, editor recommendations, products trending on social media, and long-trusted favorites, and the team tried 281 products in all. Hands-on studio experiments probed each one for durability, function, and quality. The testing also moved onto trains, planes, and cars, and editors flew to countries such as Norway and Japan. Apparel and shoes went out in New York City, around the country, and overseas. A panel of experts reviewed some of the winners and offered feedback, and most winners carry an overall score on a five-point scale. Executive Editor Adrianna Brach presented highlights on TODAY. Prices reflect the moment of publication. Some categories crown more than one winner, and the 15 that follow form a selection of the winners in an order that implies no ranking.

The Uniqlo Ultra Stretch AIRism Dress won the best travel dress award with a score of 5 out of 5, and at $39.90 it can serve as a whole outfit in a suitcase. Sneakers pair with it during the day. Sandals and a shawl carry it into the evening. The shoes and the wrap change the look, while the dress itself stays the same. Shop TODAY tagged the dress as a bestseller, and Uniqlo sells it at that price, putting a top mark within reach of a modest budget.

Quick-drying, sweat-wicking polyester suits the dress to hot destinations. Editor Shannon Garlin, who tested it this spring, said the fabric dries fast and soaks up sweat on hot days. Testers rated the material comfortable as well. A fabric that sheds moisture keeps the dress from clinging over a full day out, an essential trait in clothing worn for hours on end.

A longer hem gives the dress a second job on itineraries that include sacred sites. On Garlin's 5-foot-4-inch frame, the hem fell to about mid-calf. She liked that length, which she said makes the dress a good option for visiting sacred and holy places on a trip. Her height gives taller wearers a reference point. On a longer frame, the hem will land higher on the leg. The team favored its airy cut as well. Extra coverage, in this case, does not mean a garment that hugs the body.

The dress runs large, and editors recommend ordering a size down for a closer fit. Uniqlo offers it in five colors and sizes XXS through XL. Shoppers who want the relaxed drape can keep their usual size. A single dress that handles sweltering heat, a night out, and a visit to a place of worship lets a traveler pack fewer pieces for a varied route.

The Case-Mate Soap Bubble Waterproof Floating Pouch keeps water out to a depth of 3.3 feet, and it won the best all-weather phone protector award with a score of 4.25 out of 5. Its bestseller label adds a second endorsement, this one from shoppers spending their own money.

Adrianna Brach, Shop TODAY's executive editor, pitched the pouch as cover for more than a handset. In her description, it guards keys, an ID, cash, and other belongings against water, sand, and dirt. A day at the beach or the pool exposes all of those items at once, and a loose pile on a towel invites loss. One waterproof sleeve keeps the whole kit together.

A clear face lets an owner use the phone without breaking the seal. A fingertip can work the touchscreen through the transparent panel, so a traveler can check a map or snap a picture by the water without opening anything. The opposite face hides pockets that keep valuables out of sight, letting the pouch double as a waterproof wallet. An adjustable lanyard keeps it within reach.

Buoyancy covers the worst case. A bare phone that slips off a dock or a boat sinks, while this pouch rides on the surface until someone fishes it out.

Case-Mate built the pouch to fit all phones, which lets one model serve a group of travelers carrying different devices. It comes in 13 colors, enough for companions to tell their pouches apart. Case-Mate and Amazon $AMZN each list it at $20, and Target $TGT charges $29.99, a $9.99 premium for the same item.

The promo code TODAY takes 20% off sitewide at Case-Mate. Applied to the $20 price, the code makes the brand's own site the cheapest of the three retailers named. The sitewide reach also means the discount extends to anything else a shopper adds to the same order.

The Halfday Garment Tote won best travel tote for garments with a 5/5 score at $158 by tucking a full garment bag inside an everyday carry-all. A side zipper releases the garment bag, which holds suits, dresses, and shirts. Formal pieces ride in their own section, away from the shoes and toiletries that could crease or soil them. The setup spares a traveler from juggling a separate hanging bag alongside a tote on the way through a terminal.

The main compartment swallows a laptop, clothes, shoes, and toiletries. Editors pitched the tote for wedding weekends, quick business trips, and adventures of up to 48 hours. Each of those outings tends to call for one polished outfit next to casual basics, and the split interior lets a single bag cover both needs. On a work trip, a computer and a suit share the same piece of luggage.

A 1680D ballistic nylon exterior resists water and abrasion. The shell can shrug off a rainy curb or a scrape against an overhead bin, the kind of wear a short trip brings. Testers praised the sturdy handles and found the tote easy to haul, a meaningful result for a bag loaded with formalwear, footwear, and electronics.

The tote measures 19 inches long, 15 inches wide, and 8 inches deep, and reviewers flagged the width as a drawback. The broad profile buys room for a dress and a weekend's gear, though it can feel bulky in a crowded aisle or a cramped train car. Shoppers can pick from three colors.

Halfday has collected a Travel Award before, for its two-in-one duffel. A second win for a different bag suggests the brand's strength reaches beyond a single design. Top marks despite the complaint about its girth show that editors weighed the drawback against the two-section layout and judged the trade worth making.

The Kodak Charmera earned a 4.67 out of 5 on its way to Shop TODAY's best viral travel gadget award. The word viral in that award title marks a product whose fame spread online. It sells for $34.99 at Amazon $AMZN, Target $TGT, and Walmart $WMT. One button captures both still pictures and video clips. The keychain shooter promises the charm of old cameras with no rolls to develop.

Seven vintage-inspired filters and four frames give each shot a retro finish before it leaves the device. Behind those extras sits an f/2.4, 35mm lens. Editors listed its compact build as the lone strength in their notes, which suits a camera that hangs from a key ring.

CNBC reports that Kodak released the palm-sized point-and-shoot in partnership with the camera company Reto. Marketing casts each of the camera's seven styles as a working fashion accessory, according to CNBC. Every version carries settings that mimic the look of analog film prints. The blind box packaging hands each buyer one of seven designs at random, according to Time. Two shoppers who buy the same box can end up with different designs. A traveler set on a particular design has to accept the luck of the draw.

The Charmera arrives without an SD card, the one drawback editors flagged. Owners transfer their files from that card to a computer. The gadget needs a card before it can pull its weight on a trip. Shop TODAY recommends adding a Lexar 64GB Micro SD Card 2-Pack for $39.99 and an SD card reader for $16.99. The Lexar bundle works out to about $20 per card. Its second card leaves a spare for a longer vacation. The reader alone runs close to half the camera's price. Together those add-ons run $56.98, lifting the full kit to $91.97. The accessories end up costing more than the keychain camera they serve.

The Satechi Vegan-Leather FindAll Passport Cover, which editors named best passport cover with a score of 4 out of 5, gives a $59.99 sleeve the power to report its own whereabouts. Bluetooth connects the cover to Apple $AAPL's Find My network, and an iPhone can display the cover's location in real time. The tracking hardware lives inside the cover, so owners have no reason to slip a separate tag between the pages.

Satechi left off a charging port. The cover recharges without a cable and works with Qi chargers. Anyone who packs a Qi pad for a phone can top up the cover on the same surface. Owners can make it play a sound and share it with other people, so a companion can join the search. The cover lacks Apple's Precision Find feature, though it reports a last known position.

Executive editor Adrianna Brach tied the cover's usefulness to travel within the U.S. Travelers $TRV without a Real ID need a passport even for domestic trips, she noted. Under that requirement, the document rides along on in-country itineraries as well as overseas ones. Each added trip hands the passport another chance to go missing, the exact risk the Find My link addresses.

Slots for credit cards, cash, and boarding passes line the interior, enough for the cover to replace a wallet. RFID blocking shields the cards inside. The passport attaches to the cover by its final page, and a boarding pass can tuck in behind the cards. Satechi made the shell from vegan leather and stitched the edges to reinforce the spot most prone to wear.

The cover measures 5.6 by 4.27 by 0.66 inches and comes in three colors at Amazon $AMZN and Satechi. Folding a tracker, a wallet, and a passport holder into a package less than an inch thick leaves one fewer item to misplace on the road.

The Ekouaer Swim Dress earned Shop TODAY's best value swimsuit award with a score of 4.67 out of 5, and Amazon $AMZN lists it at $32.99, down 15% from $38.99. The markdown trims $6 from a suit priced at the low end of the award-winning swimwear. Shop TODAY tags the dress as a bestseller, a sign that readers have put money behind it alongside the testers who scored it.

The Ekouaer costs less than The Ruffle Backflip from Summersalt, the best one-piece swimsuit winner, including at the sale price Dick's lists. Deputy partnerships editor Francesca Cocchi Zabloudil found the Summersalt supportive for bigger busts, and testers credited the Ekouaer with the same strength. A shopper who needs that lift can get it at the Ekouaer's lower price. Testers flagged the Summersalt as running small, and the Ekouaer's spec sheet lists no sizing caution.

A high-rise fit carries the dress's coverage up through the midsection, beyond what a low-cut suit offers. Testers liked the slight compression in the fabric, a trait that helps a suit stay put through a long afternoon at the beach or pool.

Fixed straps marked the single drawback testers recorded. Swimmers who like to tailor how the top sits will have to live with the stock fit. The limit weighs more on a suit sold through Amazon, where a buyer cannot try it on before it arrives.

The dress comes in 24 colors and sizes S through XXL. Among all the winners, only a pair of Project Cloud flip-flops offers a wider palette, and the range lets a buyer coordinate the suit with a vacation wardrobe. At its list price, the dress undercuts the Soma Swim Caftan Cover-Up's sale price, which makes the swimsuit the cheaper half of a seaside outfit assembled from this year's winners.

Towel Crabber Towel Bands won the best beach hack award with a 4.67 out of 5 score, and a six-piece set costs $11.99 at Amazon $AMZN. Each silicone loop stretches around the top of a lounge chair and pins a towel in place. A towel anchored this way stays put through a gust that would lift a loose one off the seat. The bands appeared among the winners featured on The 3rd Hour of TODAY.

Adrianna Brach, Shop TODAY's executive editor, judged the bands a clear improvement over clips, which she called annoying. She added that the loops fit most standard chairs up to 25 inches wide. An oversized lounger beyond that span comes with no assurance of a fit.

Brach took a set on a cruise and called the bands genius for that trip as well. The upper deck, she noted, never stops blowing. Her verdict carries the product past the shoreline its award names. A strap that tames a towel on a windy ship earns space in more than one kind of suitcase.

Reviewers singled out the bands as compact and secure. Both traits serve the trip at opposite ends, one at the packing stage and the other beside the water. Each set contains six pieces, and buyers can choose from six colors. A handful of thin silicone bands claims little room in a packed bag.

Towel Crabber sells no smaller packs, the lone drawback in the review. A solo traveler who needs one band still buys all six. Split across the set, each band works out to about $2. The extra pieces add little to the bill and leave spares for a travel companion's chair.

Peak Design's $29.95 Packable Tote shrinks to 5.9 by 3.5 by 1.6 inches once folded, and it won the best packable travel tote award with a 4.67 out of 5. At that footprint, the bag can ride in a suitcase corner on the outbound leg without crowding out clothes. A spare carryall that takes up little room on day one leaves the main luggage's full capacity for the things a traveler planned to bring.

Souvenirs explain the appeal for executive editor Adrianna Brach, who said she always reaches the end of a trip needing an extra bag to hold them. She added that the tote doubles as a personal item on a plane, a role she said lets fliers sidestep extra fees. In her telling, the same object that saved space on the way out earns its keep on the way home by carrying the overflow aboard.

A honeymoon purchase sharpened her view. Brach recalled buying a bag in an airport during that trip and paying a steep price for it. She described the chance to pick up this one for $30 as a "travel PSA." Her story casts the tote as a hedge against a predictable expense. Travelers $TRV who wait until the airport to find extra space pay whatever the terminal charges, at the moment they have the fewest alternatives.

Testers praised the tote's ultra-light weight and comfortable strap, two traits that count for a bag meant to be carried full on a travel day. Its shell uses Versa Heal 70d nylon fabric, and buyers can choose from five colors. Testers recorded a single drawback. The tote cannot go in a washing machine. Owners must find another way to clean it.

Its only recorded flaw surfaces at home, after the trip ends. The lone complaint falls outside the work of hauling gear, which suggests the tote handled what testers asked of it on the road.

Shop TODAY editors approached travel pillows as skeptics, yet the Dot&Dot Twist Memory Foam Travel Pillow won them over with a 4.67 out of 5 and the award for best travel pillow. Amazon $AMZN sells it for $29.99 in five colors. A high mark from doubters says more about a product than praise from fans of the category. Judges who expected little from the category had every reason to mark this one down, and they rewarded it.

The twisting design gives one cushion three jobs. A traveler can wear it around the neck in the familiar donut shape, drape it over one shoulder, or wedge it against a window or wall. Each position suits a different way of resting in a seat. A sleeper who starts a flight upright and ends it slumped toward the cabin wall can reshape the same pillow without packing a second one. An aisle passenger with no wall within reach still keeps the neck and shoulder options.

Memory foam keeps all three shapes useful. The material springs back each time its owner switches positions, and testers listed that easy rebound among the pillow's strengths. Foam that stayed flattened after one twist would leave the other configurations limp. Quick recovery holds the whole concept together.

Reviewers gave the washable cover its own praise, a practical feature for an item that spends hours pressed against someone's neck and face. A cover that survives washing lets the pillow return from a long flight and set out clean on the next one.

The team flagged the pillow as hard to store, a fair complaint about something that still has to ride in a bag between connections. A cushion thick enough to cradle a head claims carry-on space that clothes, chargers, or snacks would compete for. The Twist solves an in-seat comfort problem and hands travelers a packing problem in exchange.

Twelve South's ButterFly SE 2-in-1 Qi2 Charger scored 5 out of 5, and Amazon $AMZN listed it for $70 at publication, 30% below its $99.99 list price. The device unfolds to reveal two charging surfaces. One holds a phone. The other powers AirPods or an Apple $AAPL Watch. A traveler can refill both gadgets overnight from a single cord.

A tester likened the folded charger to a makeup compact, and its listed dimensions run 9 by 2.4 by 2.4 inches. Buyers can pick from six colors. One folding unit that does the work of two spares a carry-on the weight and tangle of a separate stand for each gadget.

A meter-long cable ships in the box, and any standard 30W USB-C adapter will run the ButterFly SE. Editors suggested Anker's Nano USB-C Charger Block $SQ at $15.99, down from $19.99, and Apple's 30W USB-C Port Power Adapter at $39, down from $59. Pairing the Amazon deal with the Anker block brings the total to $85.99. Even with a new adapter, the package undercuts the charger's $99.99 list price on its own.

Twelve South listed the ButterFly SE at $79.99, and Apple listed it at $79.95. Amazon's price ran $9.99 below the brand's own store and $9.95 below Apple's. Testers warned that the charger may overheat. A traveler who owns a 30W USB-C brick can skip the adapter and hold the full outlay at $70.

The Ban.do 3-in-1 Game won best boredom buster with a 4/5 score by putting checkers, chess, and backgammon on a single $34.95 roll-up board.

A two-sided design lets one surface host all three games. Chess and checkers share the front, and backgammon fills the reverse. Flipping the board switches games. One flat piece takes the place of three separate boxes in a bag.

The set ships with 32 game pieces and four dice, 36 items altogether, and a zippered pocket in the board holds every one of them. Testers counted the built-in zip compartment among the set's strengths. With the pieces sealed inside, the game moves as one object. No separate pouch can go missing between a hotel room and a departure gate.

Smooth leatherette wraps the board, and Ban.do says the material wipes clean and holds up under repeated rolling. Both points matter for a game that a traveler unrolls at every stop. A surface that flexes without wearing out suits that routine. Wipe-clean material fits tray tables, picnic blankets, and other spots where crumbs and spills collect.

Spread flat, the board measures 14 inches long by 10 inches wide. Testers flagged it as hard to store, the one drawback they recorded. The complaint sits oddly beside a roll-up design, and the dimensions explain why. Rolling shrinks the footprint, yet the tube runs at least 10 inches from end to end. Packed, the game needs a slot that long, which can crowd a small personal item.

Split across three games, the price comes to less than $12 apiece. At that cost, money stops being the main hurdle. Suitcase space decides whether the set makes the trip. A traveler with room to spare gets three ways to fill a long delay from one purchase.

Soma's High-Waist Wide-Leg Pants earned 4.83 out of 5 and the award for best overall travel pant by holding their form from morning through night. The sale price of $55.30 sits 30% below the original $79.

The waistband supplies much of the appeal. A high rise applies mild compression, and the fabric gives the pants a "second skin" feel. Gentle pressure at the midsection offers support through hours in a seat without the bite of a rigid closure. The cut keeps its lines over long stretches, a trait that counts when one outfit has to carry someone from the departure gate to the dinner table.

Lower down, the leg opens into a roomy silhouette that leaves space to move in cramped rows and on city walks. Side pockets keep small essentials within reach. Three inseam lengths let shorter and taller wearers decide where the hem lands, so the wide leg can fall as intended instead of bunching at the ankle or dragging along the ground. Testers praised the light weight, an advantage for anyone trying to keep a bag lean.

Writer Jannely Espinal wears them herself, an endorsement from a staffer who chose the pants for her own closet. Soma sells the style in six colors, enough range to pair with most tops a traveler packs, and in sizes XS through XXL. The pants run big, a quirk worth weighing before choosing a size. Reviewers warned that the fabric may pill, a cosmetic drawback for a packer hoping to rotate one pair through a whole trip. Neither concern touches the comfort or shape behind the score, which points to fit and fabric wear as the probable reasons the pants stopped a fraction short of full marks.

Quince's Expandable Carry-On Suitcase scored 5/5 and won the award for most elevated carry-on at a sale price of $169.90, 48% below its $325 list price. Shop TODAY describes Quince as a brand whose products rival luxury labels at lower prices. This suitcase backs up that pitch. It pairs the maximum score with a price under $170, a markdown that trims close to half from the full retail tag.

A butterfly opening splits the carry-on into two halves for packing. A traveler can fill one half and the other, sorting belongings before the case closes. Interior compression panels pin clothing in place, and a removable laundry bag gives worn items a separate home. Editors counted the generous capacity among the bag's strengths, along with a TSA-approved lock. The expandable build named in the title points to extra room for a heavier return leg. Taken together, the panels and the laundry bag keep a carry-on orderly from the first night of a trip to the ride home.

The suitcase glides on 360-degree wheels, and editors praised its smooth roll. Wheels that swivel in any direction let a traveler steer the case upright through a crowded terminal or a narrow train aisle. A telescoping handle completes the rolling hardware and slides back down once the bag reaches its destination.

A polycarbonate shell keeps the luggage lightweight yet sturdy. The same shell scuffs with little effort, the one drawback the editors recorded. The case measures 23.03 by 15.16 by 10.24 inches and comes in eight colors. Scuffs mark the surface without changing how the case opens, holds clothes, or moves. The only cost the editors named comes down to appearance. A full score alongside a cosmetic flaw shows the testers weighted how the suitcase works above how it looks after a few outings.

Comfrt's Airplane Mode Travel Hoodie and Sweatpants each scored 5/5 to win the best travel set award, and the hoodie sells for $59, down 58% from $140. The matching sweatpants cost $49, a 30% cut from their earlier $70 tag. Editor Vivien Moon said she knew the set had beaten every rival from the moment she pulled it out of its packaging. She called every detail of the outfit "perfect," a verdict the two top scores back up.

Storage drives much of Moon's enthusiasm. She praised the set's "infinite pockets," saying travelers can tuck whatever they need into one and trust that nobody will grab their important belongings. Editors counted "plenty of pockets" among the sweatpants' strengths. The design keeps a traveler's essentials on the body, where a bag can't swallow them.

The hoodie conceals a built-in sleep mask, the feature Moon named as the best part of the set. With the mask attached, a flier has one fewer item to pack for a nap on a plane. Editors listed comfort and softness among the hoodie's virtues and credited the sweatpants with comfort as well. Moon described the pair as the comfiest set she can wear anywhere and said its softness helps her feel at ease. She went further, saying whoever designed the set deserves a kiss on the forehead and that she would not change a thing.

Both pieces come in sizes XS to 3X, and the hoodie offers 17 colors to the sweatpants' 18. The hoodie blends cotton and polyester. Testers flagged a few weak spots in the set. The hoodie does not resist odors, and the sweatpants run long and lack a drawstring. Together, the markdowns trim $102 from the $210 the two pieces once cost. At publication prices, a shopper could own the full set for $108, less than the hoodie's former price alone.

The New Balance 1080v15 won best sneaker for long walks with a score of 4.67 out of 5, and testers praised both its padded sole and its resistance to blisters. They rated the shoe comfortable too, a quality that counts for a lot on a sightseeing day measured in miles.

Writer Emma Stessman came to this pair as a longtime fan of the line. She has tried several earlier iterations of the 1080 and ranks them among her favorite everyday sneakers of all time. Her history with the shoe gives her verdict on the new model a clear point of comparison. She can measure the latest release against predecessors she knows from experience.

New Balance retired the Fresh Foam material it had used for years and swapped in an all-new type of cushioning, according to Stessman. She describes the result as bouncy. In her testing, the padding springs back to its original form with each step. Stessman framed that praise as an early read, saying she had been enjoying the bounce so far. A sole that recovers its shape stride after stride suits the long walks the award names.

The 1080v15 weighs less than the previous version, Stessman found. She called the lighter build a welcome change, the kind of improvement she always appreciates. A lighter shoe asks less of a traveler's legs over a full day, and it adds less heft to a packed suitcase.

Amazon $AMZN and Zappos list the sneaker at $169.95, and New Balance charges $169.99. It comes in 13 colors and sizes 7 to 16, and the shoe uses mesh and rubber. The upper end of that size run reaches 16, room for travelers with larger feet. Editors flagged one weakness. The materials do not resist stains.

None of the three retailers listed a markdown at publication, and a gap of four cents separates the cheapest from the priciest.

#5491. 10 Zelda games ranked by Metacritic, from Ocarina of Time to Minish Cap

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A 2017 Metacritic ordering of Zelda games lists 16 entries. Here are 10 of them, from Ocarina of Time on the N64 to Minish Cap.

Each new Zelda game that arrives to a wave of praise sets off the same argument among players over where it belongs in the series' history. Breath of the Wild, the Switch adventure, had sparked that debate by March 2017. Critics and fans were calling it one of the strongest games the franchise had produced. The acclaim raised a harder question. Could a newcomer unseat a long line of beloved adventures and claim the crown as the greatest Zelda? The series had turned 30, and the field of contenders was crowded. Settling the matter interests anyone deciding which older entries deserve their time, and it interests longtime fans who want to see a favorite vindicated.

Metacritic offers a tempting shortcut through the dispute. The site gathers verdicts from writers across the web and condenses them into a single score anyone can read at a glance. Some players trust the site, and others resent it. A lone number conceals how it came together. Two titles with similar standing might rest on pools of unequal size, and a handful of writers can carry as much weight for one release as dozens do for another. Audience opinion and professional judgment diverge as well, which shows that no composite figure can resolve a question of taste. Any ordering that draws on these scores captures a snapshot of expert opinion at one moment, and readers should weigh it that way.

GamesRadar+ turned to Metacritic for a verdict in a March 2, 2017, article by Sam Prell. The outlet's own review had held up Breath of the Wild as the benchmark other adventure games would have to clear, and Prell set out to learn what the aggregated marks revealed about the series. He declined to weigh the strengths and flaws of Metacritic's method. Prell sorted the games by their critic results, and his list prints no scores. He excluded re-releases with two exceptions. The Game Boy Advance versions of the first two games stayed in, because dropping them would have erased the original Legend of Zelda from the lineup. Twilight Princess appears on both GameCube and Wii, since its controls differ so much between the two machines. Prell cautioned that different outlets reviewed different games and that the tally of write-ups varies from title to title. Breath of the Wild had drawn 60 reviews at the time of writing, while Ocarina of Time had 22, a gap of 38. He added that user ratings put Majora's Mask ahead of Ocarina of Time, and he named Spirit Tracks as his personal favorite. His ordering covers 16 entries across 12 numbered positions, with tied games sharing a number. This article presents 10 of those entries in Metacritic's order.

Ocarina of Time holds first place in the Metacritic critic order, finishing ahead of all 15 other Zelda entries on the list, Breath of the Wild included. The N64 adventure keeps the summit to itself, with no rival sharing its number. Two of the first four positions carry a single game, and the N64 title owns the higher of them.

Its advantage spans every console represented. The ordering draws from seven platforms, and Ocarina of Time sits above every title from the other six: Switch, GameCube, Wii, 3DS, DS, and Game Boy Advance. The gap stretches widest against the Game Boy Advance editions of the series' first two games, with the original Legend of Zelda 10 places down at 11th and Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link tied for 12th.

The N64 posts the cleanest record of any multi-game console in the order. Both of its entries land inside the top four, with Majora's Mask tied for fourth. Every other system with more than one title has at least one outside that group, from Four Swords Adventures on GameCube to Tri Force Heroes on 3DS. Wii comes nearest, with Twilight Princess tied for fourth and Skyward Sword one step below in fifth. Game Boy Advance fields four entries, and A Link to the Past is the lone one to get that far.

The game's reputation reaches beyond review tallies. The Chicago Sun-Times reports that digital games curator Andrew Borman said developers around the world continue to name Ocarina of Time as an influence on their own work. Some players and critics count it among the finest video games ever made.

Across seven platforms, a single release from the Switch separates the N64 game from the rest of the series. Breath of the Wild is the one challenger critics placed within a step of Ocarina of Time.

Breath of the Wild claimed second place among 16 Zelda entries in Metacritic's critic order, and it stands as the lone Switch game on the list. Ocarina of Time, the N64 release, is the single title reviewers put above it. Each of the remaining 14 entries finished beneath the newcomer, including Majora's Mask, the other N64 adventure. Wind Waker and the GameCube version of Twilight Princess share third, the next step down. The Switch game's edge over the rest of the field spans six other consoles, from the N64 and GameCube to the Wii, DS, 3DS, and Game Boy Advance. The titles it outscored include A Link to the Past, Skyward Sword, and A Link Between Worlds.

Breath of the Wild runs on physics and weather systems that shape every outing. A tree that Link fells on a hillside will topple and roll down the slope, clearing whatever sits in its path. Boulders obey the same logic, and a well-aimed shove sends one down an incline to flatten opponents. Sudden rain can snuff out fires. A temperature gauge pushes players to change into warmer or cooler clothes to suit their surroundings.

Combat and exploration demand the same improvisation. Axes, clubs, and long blades break with little use, and Link can grab replacements from the enemies he faces. Foes live in colonies and encampments instead of wandering at random. They sleep at night, which lets a patient hunter sneak up on them. Link has a dedicated jump button and can climb any vertical surface he reaches, from ruins and towers to cliff walls and tree trunks.

Finishing one notch behind the N64 benchmark puts the Switch debut in contention for the title of greatest Zelda. Prell drew a more modest conclusion. He closed his piece by saying the order made one point seem clear, that Breath of the Wild is "one very good game."

Wind Waker shares third place with the GameCube edition of Twilight Princess, which makes GameCube the only console with two games among the first three positions on Metacritic's Zelda list. Ocarina of Time holds the first spot for the Nintendo 64, and Breath of the Wild claims the second for Switch. Every other platform in the source's 16 entries has to wait until fourth place or lower to appear.

The tie leaves Wind Waker one step behind Breath of the Wild and ahead of a three-way logjam at fourth that includes Majora's Mask and A Link to the Past. GameCube's run near the summit ends with Wind Waker and Twilight Princess. Four Swords Adventures, the third GameCube release in the list, lands 10th, seven spots beneath Wind Waker. The same hardware produced both a third-place tie and a 10th-place finish in critics' eyes.

Wind Waker's story jumps several hundred years past the events of Ocarina of Time and follows an adventure aboard a pirate ship across a world covered by sea, according to TIME. One TIME reviewer described the cartoon-like graphics as smooth and detailed. The review singled out heat haze from flames and the wet footprints the hero leaves behind after emerging from the sea.

Wind Waker's stylized, cartoony Link drew fire from part of the audience. Some gamers criticized the redesign as a step backward for the series. The look went on to earn the game several awards for visual design.

Every handheld entry on the list sits below Wind Waker, including A Link to the Past on Game Boy Advance in the fourth-place group. The GameCube adventure finishes two spots ahead of Skyward Sword, the Wii release in fifth, and three ahead of A Link Between Worlds, the strongest 3DS entry at sixth. Only two entries outrank Wind Waker, and 12 finish behind it. A Link to the Past, the best handheld showing, has four entries above it, twice the count ahead of Wind Waker.

Twilight Princess appears twice in the Metacritic order, with its GameCube edition tied for third and its Wii edition tied for fourth. No other game among the 16 entries holds more than one slot.

The GameCube release shares third with Wind Waker. Ocarina of Time and Breath of the Wild are the sole games above that pair. The GameCube version beats every handheld entry in the order, including A Link to the Past on Game Boy Advance, the strongest portable performer. Four Swords Adventures, the third GameCube title, lands in the bottom half of the list, trailing both of its console mates.

The Wii release slips one step, into a three-way tie with Majora's Mask on N64 and A Link to the Past on Game Boy Advance. The deadlock spans three machines, the N64, the Wii, and the Game Boy Advance. Seven entries fill the first four positions, and two of them carry the Twilight Princess name. The editions occupy adjacent levels, a sign that critics regarded the two versions in similar terms while giving the GameCube edition the edge.

No handheld game climbs above the Wii version. A Link to the Past, its lone portable peer at fourth, matches it without surpassing it.

Twilight Princess builds its challenges around animal allies and magnetism. Players rescue a family of monkeys who help solve clockwork puzzles. Another section hands over heavy iron boots that let the player stride across magnetized walls and ceilings.

The Wii edition finishes one spot ahead of Skyward Sword, the other Wii game on the list, which holds fifth alone. Nine entries sit beneath the Wii edition, from Skyward Sword down to the two games tied for last. Twilight Princess owns the Wii's best critical showing and a share of the GameCube's. No other entry earns top billing on two consoles.

Majora's Mask holds a share of fourth on the Metacritic list, level with Twilight Princess on Wii and A Link to the Past on Game Boy Advance. Four entries finish ahead of the trio, and nine of the source's 16 land beneath the group. The tie unites three different machines, pairing a Nintendo 64 adventure with a Wii release and a handheld title. Critic esteem at this tier crossed the line between living-room hardware and the portables players carry.

Nintendo 64 games claim two of the first four spots, with Ocarina of Time at the summit and Majora's Mask three steps lower. The pair make up the whole Nintendo 64 contingent in the order, so the platform landed every one of its Zelda entries in the top group.

Majora's Mask outpaces seven of the eight portable games on the list. Its tie partner, A Link to the Past, is the one handheld release to match it. A Link Between Worlds, Phantom Hourglass, Minish Cap, Spirit Tracks, the original Legend of Zelda, Tri Force Heroes, and Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link all trail. Spirit Tracks finishes five places beneath Majora's Mask, and Tri Force Heroes and Zelda 2 share the bottom rung.

Majora's Mask builds its adventure around a Groundhog Day-like loop. Players repeat the same stretch of time and keep their progress, while non-player characters lose their memories with each reset.

Eiji Aonuma explained that reusing Ocarina of Time character models in Majora's Mask served in part to save development time. He called the reuse a stylistic decision as well. Familiar characters, he said, could express different things in a world that felt like another dimension.

Every Nintendo 64 game in Prell's lineup falls inside the upper third of its 12 numbered positions, a record no other system with two or more entries can claim.

A Link to the Past shares fourth place in Metacritic's Zelda order with Majora's Mask on the N64 and the Wii edition of Twilight Princess, and it is the only Game Boy Advance title in that three-way tie. Critics judged a GBA release the equal of games on two home consoles. The tie gathers a single handheld game alongside two home-console releases, and the shared number gives none of the three an edge.

Game Boy Advance titles account for four of the 16 entries, and A Link to the Past finishes ahead of the other three. Minish Cap lands eighth, four positions lower. The GBA version of the original Legend of Zelda sits 11th, seven spots back. Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link shares the bottom rung at 12th with Tri Force Heroes. All three occupy the lower half of the list's numbered positions, and A Link to the Past holds the only GBA spot in the upper half. Critics scattered these four games from fourth to last despite their common hardware. The platform set no ceiling on a game's reach.

Seven of the 16 entries hold fourth or better, and A Link to the Past is the lone GBA game in that leading group. The other six run on the N64, the GameCube, the Switch, or the Wii. The GBA game's nearest neighbors below the tie come from other systems. Skyward Sword on the Wii follows at fifth, and the 3DS release A Link Between Worlds is next at sixth. Releases on the Wii, the 3DS, and the DS fill the gap between A Link to the Past and the next GBA game.

Phantom Hourglass and Spirit Tracks, the two DS games, trail A Link to the Past by three and five steps. Eight titles on the list belong to the GBA, the DS, or the 3DS, and A Link to the Past is the sole member of that set to finish above sixth. The other seven all fall behind every game in the fourth-or-better tier. On critic verdicts, no DS or 3DS game matched the strongest GBA entry.

Skyward Sword holds fifth place by itself in the Metacritic critic order, the first entry since Breath of the Wild at second to claim a position without a partner. Seven entries finish above it, and eight more fall beneath it. The Wii release sits at the hinge of the list, with five of the seven tied entries packed into the upper ranks.

Twilight Princess on Wii stands one step higher, inside the three-way logjam at fourth with Majora's Mask and A Link to the Past. Skyward Sword ends up as the lower of the two Wii games in the lineup. The GameCube edition of Twilight Princess shares third, so Twilight Princess finishes ahead of Skyward Sword in both of its versions.

The adventure opens with Link as a pupil at a flying school in Skyloft, a town that floats in the sky. Reviewers called the story a kind of earlier chapter to Ocarina of Time. They pointed out that the series, which tends to keep its tales separate, had not linked games that way before. The prequel thread binds Skyward Sword to Ocarina of Time. Four rungs separate the pair in Metacritic's standings. Skyward Sword trims the count of key locations compared with previous Zelda games, and it asks players to return to each one with new items or abilities that bring different enemies, challenges, and secrets.

Four Swords Adventures on GameCube, at 10th, is the lone home-console entry below Skyward Sword. Every other title in the bottom half, from A Link Between Worlds on 3DS at sixth down to Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link at the shared 12th, belongs to the Game Boy Advance, DS, or 3DS. Handheld systems account for seven of the eight entries in that half. Skyward Sword marks the last home-console release in the top half of the 16-entry field.

A Link Between Worlds holds sixth place in the Metacritic order, the strongest critic standing of any DS or 3DS game on the list. Skyward Sword on the Wii sits one step above it, and A Link to the Past on the Game Boy Advance stands as the lone portable title ahead of it.

Both DS games land beneath the 3DS release. Phantom Hourglass trails by one notch at seventh, and Spirit Tracks falls three places lower, at ninth. Critics in aggregate preferred the 3DS adventure to either DS game.

Its 3DS stablemate sank to the bottom. Tri Force Heroes shares 12th, the last spot in the field, six numbered ranks below A Link Between Worlds. Two games on the same hardware landed at opposite ends of the critic verdicts, evidence that the platform by itself did not decide where a game finished.

Game Boy Advance entries scatter on both sides of the 3DS adventure. A Link to the Past shares fourth with two home-console games, and Minish Cap sits two spots back at eighth. The GBA versions of the original Legend of Zelda and Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link land at 11th and in a tie for 12th. Among the eight GBA, DS, and 3DS entries on the list, A Link Between Worlds claims the second-best result.

Home-console hardware offered no guarantee of a higher placing. Four Swords Adventures, a GameCube release, lands at 10th, four rungs behind the 3DS title. Wind Waker and the GameCube edition of Twilight Princess share third, so the 3DS game sits between GameCube releases seven places apart.

Ties among higher entries push A Link Between Worlds deeper into the field than its number suggests. Eight of the 16 entries sit ahead of it, and seven sit behind it. Counted entry by entry, the 3DS game is the ninth of 16 and opens the bottom half.

Phantom Hourglass claims seventh in the Metacritic order, two rungs above Spirit Tracks, the lone other DS entry among the 16 games on the list. Critics split the DS pair, placing one game in the middle of the pack and dropping its sibling to ninth, with Minish Cap wedged between them.

Nine games finish ahead of the DS title, and they span six platforms: the N64, GameCube, Wii, Switch, GBA, and 3DS. Its closest neighbor above, A Link Between Worlds on 3DS, holds sixth. Minish Cap on GBA follows in eighth. Three different systems fill three back-to-back positions in this stretch of the order.

Six titles trail Phantom Hourglass. Minish Cap and Spirit Tracks come next. Below them sit Four Swords Adventures on GameCube, the GBA version of the original Legend of Zelda, and the pair tied for 12th, Tri Force Heroes and Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link. Phantom Hourglass finishes three positions above Four Swords Adventures, the weakest of the three GameCube titles. Seventh lands on the lower side of the midpoint across the 12 numbered positions, and the game stands 10th of 16 when each entry gets its own slot.

Eight of the 16 entries come from the GBA, DS, and 3DS. Two of those handheld games, A Link to the Past and A Link Between Worlds, finish above Phantom Hourglass. Critics placed the DS game ahead of five of the other seven portable releases, including three of the four GBA titles on the list. Spirit Tracks, the weaker DS title, sits three places above Tri Force Heroes on 3DS.

Sam Prell named Spirit Tracks, the DS game two places lower, as his favorite Zelda. He expected pushback on the choice, tacking "Yeah, I said it" onto the admission. The critic aggregate favored Phantom Hourglass, which shows that one writer's loyalty and the pooled verdict can part ways inside a single console's library.

Minish Cap, a Game Boy Advance release, finishes eighth in Metacritic's critic order, three spots above the GBA edition of the original Legend of Zelda at 11th. On a shared console, critics favored a later chapter over the adventure that started the series.

Four GBA titles appear among the 16 entries, and Minish Cap claims the second-best result of the four. A Link to the Past shares fourth, four places higher. Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link sits in the tie for 12th, four rungs lower. The GBA group stretches from the upper tier of the list to its final pair, and Minish Cap occupies the exact midpoint of that spread.

The two lowest GBA entries are the series' first two games, and neither cracks the top 10. On this handheld, the founding pair sits at the bottom, while the later adventures, A Link to the Past in its tie for fourth and Minish Cap at eighth, finish above them. Seniority earned no reward from these critics.

Minish Cap clears a home-console release as well. Four Swords Adventures on GameCube lands 10th, two places back. Spirit Tracks on DS falls between those two games at ninth, one position below Minish Cap. Phantom Hourglass, the other DS entry, sits one step ahead of Minish Cap in seventh. A Game Boy Advance game lands between two DS titles and above a GameCube one. Three different machines interleave across these four consecutive positions.

GameCube entries run from a tie for third down to 10th. Their seven-place spread rivals the eight places the GBA group covers. Wind Waker and Four Swords Adventures shared a console, yet critics set them far apart. Both the handheld and the living-room console scatter their Zelda games across much of the order. The machine a Zelda game ran on offers no guide to where critics placed it.

#5490. Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 2, 2026 at 8:22 am

KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.

The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.

There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.

Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.

A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

Update: Late Friday afternoon KEXP said it was still working to restore services, but it did manage to put up a temporary livestream on its site.

Update: KEXP CEO Ethan Raup details what went wrong and how it was fixed in this post on LinkedIn.

#5489. ADNOC to expand AI use across its operations to strengthen resilience

Many of the biggest names in the oil and gas industry have converged on Abu Dhabi this week to attend the emirate’s flagship annual energy conference, ADIPEC, with energy security a priority as the industry grapples with ongoing supply disruptions amid heightened geopolitical tensions.

Concerns over renewed U.S. strikes on Iran and the prospect of retaliatory action by Tehran have gripped oil markets in recent days. They also led both Exxon’s CEO Darren Woods and Chevron’s upstream president, Clay Neff, to withdraw from attending ADIPEC, citing security concerns.

But overall, the turnout has been strong, with heavyweights such as BP’s CEO Meg O’Neill, Baker Hughes CEO Lorenzo Simonelli, and Halliburton’s chairman and CEO Jeff Miller, all flying in to speak at the event.

Shell, TotalEnergies, Eni, ExxonMobil, Chevron, and Occidental Petroleum were also present among the 2,260 exhibiting companies. More than 120 U.S. companies are exhibiting this year, second only to China in number. In total, the event is expected to draw around 239,000 visitors from 170 countries.

Dr Sultan Al Jaber, UAE minister of industry and advanced technology and Group CEO of ADNOC, took to the podium during the event’s opening ceremony on Monday to set the tone for the days ahead.

“Energy leadership is not measured by what you produce in good times, it is measured by what you deliver in hard times,” he said. “The choices we make today will determine the energy landscape a decade from now.”

He urged increased investment in energy infrastructure and AI to strengthen the industry’s long-term resilience against future disruptions, noting how AI has become essential to ensuring operational continuity.

“AI must be built in, not bolted on,” he said. “In a crisis, the speed of insight and the speed of decision-making is the difference between continuity and disruption.”

Earlier that morning, ADNOC signed a deal with OpenAI and G42, an Abu Dhabi-backed AI firm, to become the world’s first energy company to deploy OpenAI’s Frontier platform to build and manage AI agents. It plans to use the technology to transform its oilfield development, well management, and commercial operations.

Referring to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was seated in the front row at the ceremony as guest of honor, Al Jaber said: “Sam, from the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI. And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.”

BP’s CEO Meg O’Neill also outlined her company’s focus on AI in a speech delivered on the first day of ADIPEC.

“Understanding the macro impact of these investments and technologies, and what it means for global energy demand is really important, and we spend quite a bit of time on that, trying to sift through the myriad of forecasts which range from gentle growth to something that is astronomical and hard to figure out, and how they underpin our investment decisions,” she said.

O’Neill explained that the two main areas where BP is focusing its AI efforts are sub-surface analysis, including seismic processing and reservoir management, and the application of physical AI to improve facility operations, reduce costs and maximise resource flows through its systems.

Nine out of 10 energy leaders (89%) increased their AI spending over the past year, while 63% expect returns from existing investments to match or exceed their costs, according to the Powering Possible report, the third annual study conducted by ADNOC, its international investment arm XRG, and Microsoft.

The report, published last week, also noted how the proportion of energy leaders ranking AI among their top two corporate priorities has increased to 62%, up from 42% a year earlier, as the industry increasingly embraces agentic AI.

In addition to AI and energy security, conversations over the last few days have focused on addressing some of the sector’s most pressing challenges, including shifting trade routes to rising electricity demand and the investment needed to build resilient energy infrastructure.

Speaking to Fortune contributor Inzamam Rashid on the sidelines of ADIPEC, Dr Carole Nakhle, CEO of Crystol Energy and Secretary General of the Arab Energy Club, described the scale of this year’s energy disruption as “unprecedented”.

“We are all sailing through a very thick fog,” Nakhle said. “Resilience doesn’t get parachuted in overnight; it requires investment over years and decades.”

Melissa HancockAnd as ever, thanks for reading, and do keep in touch with your thoughts and ideas.melissa.hancock@fortune.com

Saudi state oil giant Aramco reported a net profit of $36.25 billion in the third quarter, a 34.5% increase compared with the same period a year earlier, as higher crude oil and fuel prices offset supply disruptions.

Adjusted net income in the third quarter was $31.2 billion, comfortably beating a $28.7 billion analyst consensus estimate compiled by Bloomberg.

In addition to the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, Aramco’s facilities have come under attack from Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.

Despite the attacks, supply reliability was 97.8% in the quarter, down from 99.9% a year earlier and 98.4% in the second quarter.

“This strong supply reliability was ‌achieved despite ⁠some disruptions to the East-West Pipeline during the quarter, as Aramco was able to quickly restore loadings in the western region using the pipeline's multiline configuration,” Aramco said.

Saudi Arabia’s oil production stood at around 8 million barrels per day (bpd) in September, down from just over 10 million bpd before the war, according to secondary sources cited in OPEC’s latest monthly report.

Speaking during an earnings conference call on Tuesday, Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said the company plans to increase oil production to full capacity in the fourth quarter, noting that supplies from both the Red Sea and the Gulf had already been increased.

In Aramco’s results statement, Nasser emphasized the company’s ongoing efforts to expand overseas storage capacity and identify alternative export routes, further bolstering its global supply network.

Aramco’s adjusted earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) in the downstream division soared by 234% year-on-year, driven by stronger refining margins.

Other energy majors have also posted bumper third-quarter earnings, driven by a spike in refining profits and elevated oil and gas prices. Exxon more than doubled its year-on-year third-quarter profit to $15.4 billion while Chevron’s earnings increased to $9.9 billion from $3.5 billion a year ago.

Amid reports that the U.S. may resume attacks on Iran, former Barclays CEO Bob Diamond tells Fortune that business activity across the region continues strongly and that he remains bullish on the Gulf.

“If you take the time to get here and you’re on the ground, it’s business as usual. People are investing. The region isn’t hiding in their bunker; they’re doing business,” Diamond told my colleague Kamal Ahmed on a call from Bahrain where he has been attending the Gateway Gulf investment conference.

Diamond was in the kingdom to announce the opening of Panmure Liberum’s first regional office. His investment vehicle, Atlas Merchant Capital, acquired Panmure Gordon for £15.5 million ($21 million) in 2017 before merging it with Liberum in 2024.

Bahrain offers an attractive base for building an advisory business, according to Diamond, because of its highly-regulated banking sector. Middle-market and family-owned businesses “are dying for cover,” he said, adding that the kingdom also offers a gateway to the rest of the GCC.

He also highlighted Bahrain’s opportunities in fintech, particularly stablecoins and asset tokenization.

You can read Kamal’s full interview with Diamond here

Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said concluded a landmark visit to Beijing on Monday where he met Chinese president Xi Jinping. It marked the first-ever visit by an Omani head of state to China since the two countries established diplomatic relations in 1978.

During his talks with Sultan Haitham, Xi said relations between the two countries were at a “new historical starting point,” while Sultan Haitham said Oman was open to striking a preferential trade and investment agreement with China.

The two leaders witnessed the signing of a currency swap arrangement, and multiple agreements and strategic investment partnerships with Chinese institutions and companies worth several billion dollars.

The agreements cover efforts to attract Chinese industrial and technological capabilities to Oman, as well as the establishment of joint investment funds across various fields, including renewable energy, AI, digital technologies, space, and defence.

Key among these was a preliminary terms agreement between the Oman sovereign wealth fund and China’s Silk Road Fund to establish a joint investment fund with capital of 307.6 million Omani rials (RO) ($800 million).

Preliminary statistics from the National Centre for Statistics and Information indicate that total trade during the first seven months of 2026 reached RO 5.4 billion ($14.04 billion), with Omani exports to China of about RO 3.9 billion ($10.14 billion), and imports from China of approximately RO 1.4 billion ($3.64 billion).

Imports from China accounted for 13.73% of Oman's total commodity imports over the same period. China remains Oman’s largest trading partner, while Oman is China's fourth-largest trading partner among Arab countries and its fifth-largest supplier of crude oil.

In light of the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, China views Oman as an increasingly strategic trading partner, given that many of its ports lie outside the strait.

Bahrain-based global private equity firm Arcapita Group plans to invest $1.5 billion across the Gulf’s industrial and logistics sector over the next two years. The planned investment comes on top of the more than $2 billion in industrial real estate assets the firm already manages across the region.

Gulf countries have an opportunity to turn the Syrian refugee crisis into a driver of regional economic growth, rather than relying on increasingly stretched humanitarian aid. With more than 3.8 million Syrians still living in neighboring countries, this article calls for greater economic inclusion through employment rights, access to finance, business opportunities, and freedom of movement. Syrian refugees could play an important role in Gulf-backed infrastructure and trade projects across the Levant, bringing valuable skills, commercial networks and expertise that could also support Syria’s eventual reconstruction.

#5488. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”

#5487. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5486. What Clients Need Before They Trust You With Sensitive Work

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your clients, and potential clients, need to know that they can trust you with their confidential information.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Confidentiality is essential. Without proper protection, sensitive personal or business information can become public. Cybersecurity tools and practical safeguards are critical for protecting confidential data. What assurances do your clients need before trusting you with sensitive work?

Every company seeks credibility. Building a strong reputation takes years, but a data breach or employee error can erase it instantly.

Business plans are drafted with intricate details on how a service or product will be offered. Features and benefits are discussed at length, alongside profit projections. However, few business proposals address building and protecting the company’s reputation. Why? Because entrepreneurs assume if they provide a quality product or service, that consumer trust will follow.

When I started my transcription company, I quickly realized protecting sensitive data would be our top priority. Our service is not a simple transaction. Clients entrust us with audio or video files containing sensitive information. Whether the content is for a select audience or public release, we safeguard every file as if it were confidential.

Handling sensitive data requires safeguards both inside and outside the company. Companies often require new hires to sign non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), but reputations can still be damaged if employees violate these agreements and share confidential information.

Recent headlines report charges against a foreign national accused of planting listening devices in a corporate boardroom. This case involves unauthorized recording of confidential information at a major AI company planning to go public. Both executives and future shareholders need assurance that sensitive information will remain secure.

Clients need assurance that their information will be protected. While some businesses still accept cash, most rely on electronic payments, and customers expect trusted vendors to handle their data securely.

The same applies to transcription. Secure file upload and transfer are essential. I frequently remind clients not to email files. Work for legal and medical clients must comply with CJIS and HIPAA requirements to protect sensitive data. Any breach would harm our reputation.

Industries like legal, medical and technology must protect sensitive data, but every business should prioritize customer data protection. Safeguarding information, from credit card transactions to medical histories, matters just as much across all sectors.

No matter your industry, reassure customers and clients that protecting sensitive data is a top priority. Here are a few ways to convey the importance of safeguarding customer info:

Clients and customers lose trust in companies for various reasons. Often, companies don’t realize this erosion until sales decline or complaints rise, making recovery harder. Key reasons for lost trust include:

Unfortunately, many customers are skeptical of marketing claims because products or services sometimes fail to meet expectations. When this happens, customers incur extra costs to resolve issues, and companies lose revenue through replacements or additional service.

Ethical decline is another concern. Clients become frustrated when companies fail to deliver on their promises, which underscores the importance of consistent, honest communication.

When discussing service commitments, I strive for clarity in writing, email and phone conversations. However, clients may sometimes overlook or misunderstand service details, either by not listening or reading disclosures. Following up and confirming information by email helps protect both parties.

The greatest cost of a data breach is reputational damage. While ransom payments and IT expenses are straightforward to calculate, the long-term reputational impact can cost millions over several years.

Minimizing data breach risk should be a top priority for every company. For this reason, my company employs only U.S.-based individuals who undergo comprehensive criminal background checks.

Many hackers and scammers who obtain confidential information operate overseas. I am often surprised when competitors use contractors abroad to transcribe files. Clients should know who can access their data and where those individuals are located.

Every company, regardless of size, should maintain an up-to-date data breach plan. Hackers often target small businesses as entry points to larger networks. I recommend a six-step plan:

Developing a comprehensive data breach plan requires specialized expertise. However, I recognize the importance of data security and take extensive measures to protect the sensitive information our clients entrust to us. Ultimately, all data is important to your clients and customers.

Regardless of the cause, how your company responds to failure is crucial. Mistakes happen, and even the most diligent employees or companies can “drop the ball.”

When mistakes are made, transparency matters. Be honest and admit your mistakes. Even the most irritated customer can moderate their views when a company admits its errors.

Recently, I was dining at a restaurant with high ratings for its food and service. Nonetheless, four- and five-star reviews aren’t worth much when your experience is going south. From the moment I entered the restaurant, nothing went well.

First, the host could not find my reservation, even after I provided the confirmation number. After being seated, we waited 10 minutes for our server. To speed things up, we ordered all courses at once, and the server assured us he would pace the meal appropriately.

Despite these efforts, the dining experience did not improve. When the server noticed my frustration, he brought the manager, and both apologized. The manager comped our meal, offered a premium bottle of wine and gave me a $100 gift certificate. This response changed my perspective, and when I returned the following week, the manager personally thanked me for giving them another chance.

A disappointing restaurant experience is minor compared to a multi-million-dollar mistake or data breach. However, the fundamentals of response remain the same.

Transparency and honesty are essential, but customers will only give companies a second chance if they believe their mistakes can, and will be corrected. Most importantly, customers want to feel that your company genuinely cares about them.

#5485. The midterms won’t ease borrowing costs. Here’s what CFOs should do now

Good morning. What do the U.S. midterm election results mean for finance leaders? With Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress, companies could face greater scrutiny of issues such as AI investment and data center development. But the broader financing challenges facing finance chiefs extend beyond the shifting political landscape.

“CFOs should go into 2027 expecting sustained higher borrowing costs,” Josh Putnam, EY-Parthenon’s global and Americas corporate finance leader, told me. Financing conditions are also likely to remain volatile, regardless of which party controls Congress.

Growing deficits, strong capital demand, inflation volatility, and policy uncertainty are putting pressure on long-term rates, Putnam said, making disciplined capital allocation, debt management, and investment decisions increasingly important for finance chiefs.

His advice is to stress-test investment hurdles, evaluate debt maturities, and protect balance-sheet flexibility. Companies must understand which investments can generate returns above their cost of capital and redirect resources when they cannot, he said.

Political gridlock could add risk, but on its own it does not necessarily mean higher long-term borrowing costs.

A divided government “would not automatically push term premiums higher,” said Gregory Daco, EY-Parthenon’s chief economist. But repeated budget disagreements, shutdown risks, debt ceiling stress, and greater fiscal uncertainty “would reinforce upward pressure,” he said.

Daco recommends testing investments against a range of financing costs and maintaining hurdle rates that reflect a structurally higher and more volatile cost of capital.

For companies, however, the risks extend beyond long-term interest rates. Political uncertainty can also affect access to credit and the cost of short-term financing.

“Markets respond to uncertainty by charging more, whether the risk originates in Washington, D.C., or on Wall Street,” said Mark Williams, a master lecturer in finance at Boston University’s Questrom School of Business and a former bank examiner for the Federal Reserve Bank.

Williams said that banks react to elevated risk by tightening credit terms and reducing lending. “Legislative gridlock can create volatile funding cycles and cause short-term borrowing costs to spike,” he explained. Companies relying on commercial paper, a form of short-term corporate borrowing, should consider longer-term funding, diversify financing sources, and secure credit lines across multiple banks, he said.

Because a divided government can increase the risk of shutdowns, which can delay the release of economic data, CFOs should also develop internal models to fill those gaps, Williams said. Government contractors, meanwhile, should evaluate how potential payment delays could affect cash flow.

AI investment could face particularly intense financial scrutiny as financing costs rise and regulatory uncertainty increases.Voters on Tuesday sent a clear message about the AI buildout: the costs of data centers are now a political issue. Candidates in both parties who campaigned on rising electric bills won key races, and at least 14 Ohio towns passed restrictions on data center development, Fortune reported.

The results underscore the growing regulatory and political uncertainty facing AI and data center developers, which could drive up costs and complicate project financing, Williams said. Private credit funds, the primary lenders in the space, would demand higher interest rates, he said, and prices on outstanding AI bonds could fall as yields rise.

But the market was already recalibrating AI risk before the election, Williams noted. He recommends returning to corporate finance fundamentals, including more conservative net present value assumptions, multi-variable scenario analysis, and stress testing against higher borrowing costs and stricter lending covenants.

Daco also sees a political dimension. With affordability central to the election, “a backlash is likely if households see AI investment raising power costs while its benefits remain concentrated,” he said.

CFOs should prioritize projects with measurable productivity gains, account fully for power and infrastructure costs, and pair technology investment with investment in workers and skills, Daco said.

The financial discipline required to navigate the next economic cycle remains vital. As Putnam put it, “Companies that demonstrate they can put capital to work effectively will be best positioned to pursue growth.”

Gartner suggests a strategy-first approach: identify critical capabilities, forecast future workloads, assess human and AI capacity, and evaluate workforce investments based on cost, risk, and speed. The main takeaway is that businesses should determine the right combination of people and technology to deliver results, rather than treating AI adoption primarily as an opportunity to cut staff.
